items.name: Flat bench
items.description: A padded flat bench at about knee height. The base for bench presses, dumbbell rows, hip thrusts and step-ups.
items.buying_tips: A rock-solid frame and grippy pad matter more than features; 43 cm height and 28–30 cm pad suit most.

items.name: Incline bench
items.description: A fixed bench set at about 30–45 degrees, usually with bar uprights. For incline barbell and dumbbell presses.
items.buying_tips: At home an adjustable bench covers this.

items.name: Decline bench
items.description: A bench set head-down at about 15–30 degrees with leg rollers. For decline presses and decline sit-ups.
items.buying_tips: Make sure the leg rollers lock your feet securely.
items.safety: Use a spotter for heavy barbell decline work.

items.name: Seated chest press machine
items.description: Seated machine that presses handles forward on a guided path; selectorised versions are the gym staple, plate-loaded and home-multi versions also exist.
items.adjustability: Seat height and start-position handle adjust; many have neutral and wide grips.
items.buying_tips: Look for independent (iso-lateral) arms and a start-position adjuster so you can get a full stretch.
items.safety: Set the seat so handles line up with mid-chest to protect the shoulders.

items.name: Lying chest press machine
items.description: Machine that mimics a bench press lying on your back, with lever arms you press up; usually plate loaded (Hammer Strength style), some selectorised.
items.weight_options: Plate-loaded arms; selectorised versions ~100–140 kg stack
items.adjustability: Fixed bench; some have adjustable foot assist or handle positions.
items.buying_tips: Plate-loaded iso-lateral units let each side work independently and are easier to load heavy.
items.safety: Use the stop/catch position before loading plates on one side.

items.name: Pec deck / fly machine
items.description: Seated machine with arms or pads that sweep together in front of you for a chest fly; many double as a rear-delt reverse fly.
items.weight_options: Stack ~70–110 kg; home multi versions lighter
items.adjustability: Seat height, arm start position; combo units rotate for rear delts.
items.buying_tips: A pec deck / rear delt combo saves floor space and covers both movements.
items.safety: Don't let the arms pull your shoulders past a comfortable stretch.

items.name: Incline press machine
items.description: Machine that presses up and forward at an incline to target the upper chest; selectorised or plate loaded.
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; some have multiple grips.
items.buying_tips: A seat-height adjustment matters most here: too low and it turns into a shoulder press.
items.safety: Keep shoulder blades back against the pad as you press.

items.name: Dip belt
items.description: A belt with a chain that hangs plates or a kettlebell from the hips, to add weight to dips, pull-ups and belt squats.
items.buying_tips: Leather or nylon with a long chain; check it can take kettlebells too.

items.name: Push-up board
items.description: A folding board with colour-coded slots for handles that changes the hand position to bias chest, shoulders or triceps.
items.buying_tips: Pick one with a solid hinge; you can get the same positions on the floor.

items.name: Push-up handles
items.description: Small handles that keep the wrists neutral and add range to push-ups.
items.buying_tips: Non-slip feet matter more than rotation.
items.safety: Grip firmly; rotating handles can twist under fatigue.

items.name: FID bench
items.description: An adjustable bench that goes flat, incline and decline, usually with a leg holder for decline sit-ups and presses.
items.buying_tips: Check stability in decline and that the leg holder doesn't get in the way flat.

items.name: Olympic bench with uprights
items.description: A flat bench with built-in bar uprights (and often spotter catches) for bench pressing without a rack.
items.buying_tips: Look for spotter catches; cheap home versions with leg attachments wobble.
items.safety: Use spotter catches or a spotter; a fixed bench cannot save you from a failed rep.

items.name: Rack dip attachment
items.description: Dip handles that slot onto a rack upright for dips and knee raises.
items.buying_tips: Y-shaped handles allow different widths.
items.keywords: dip attachment rack dip bars station

items.name: Bench press boards
items.description: Stacked boards placed on the chest to shorten the range of motion for board presses and overload lockout.
items.buying_tips: Foam bench blocks with straps (e.g. bench block) are easier to use alone.
items.safety: Use a spotter; boards can shift.

items.name: Competition bench
items.description: A heavy flat bench built to IPF spec (42–45 cm high, wide pad) for powerlifting bench press with stable leg drive.
items.buying_tips: Wider 30 cm pad and grippy vinyl help; must fit inside your rack.
items.keywords: competition bench ipf powerlifting wide pad

items.name: Converging chest press
items.description: Selectorised chest press whose arms move inward as you press, matching the natural adduction path of the chest.
items.adjustability: Seat height and start-position adjust; independent arms.
items.buying_tips: Usually sold as the premium version of a brand's chest press; worth it if you only buy one.
items.safety: Start light to learn the arc.

items.name: Decline press machine
items.description: Machine pressing on a downward path to bias the lower chest; plate-loaded iso-lateral and selectorised versions exist.
items.buying_tips: Less common than flat or incline; check the thigh hold-down fits your leg length.
items.safety: Set the seat so the handles start at lower-chest level.

items.name: Duffalo / bow bar
items.description: A barbell with a deep bow in the centre, letting the hands go lower on bench or wrap around the back on squats.
items.buying_tips: Mainly for powerlifting gyms; the bend gives extra bench range of motion.

items.name: Flexible / tsunami bar
items.description: A bendy bar (composite or bamboo) with plates or kettlebells hung from bands, so the load oscillates. Trains stability for bench, squat and press.
items.weight_options: Bar 2–7 kg; loaded with plates or hung kettlebells
items.adjustability: Hang load from bands for more instability.
items.buying_tips: Bamboo bars with band-hung kettlebells are cheaper; tsunami bars take plates directly.
items.safety: Use light weights; the oscillation makes sudden loss of control possible.
items.keywords: tsunami bamboo earthquake bandbell oscillating flex bar

items.name: Multi-angle press machine
items.description: Press machine whose back pad or arms adjust from flat to incline to overhead, covering chest and shoulder pressing in one station.
items.adjustability: Back angle and seat height adjust.
items.buying_tips: Great space-saver for small gyms; check the angle change is quick and needs no tools.
items.safety: Recheck seat height every time you change the angle.

items.name: Plate-loaded chest press
items.description: Seated chest press driven by independent lever arms that you load with plates, giving a free-weight feel on a fixed arc.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.buying_tips: Check the arms converge (move inward) as you press; that suits most people's shoulders.
items.safety: Unload plates evenly so the arms don't swing when you get off.
items.keywords: iso lateral chest press hammer strength

items.name: Plate-loaded incline press
items.description: Plate-loaded incline press with independent converging arms for upper-chest pressing.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.buying_tips: Pick one with a foot-assist or low start so you can get into position under heavy load.
items.safety: Load and unload alternating sides to keep the frame balanced.

items.name: Slingshot
items.description: Elastic sleeves worn over the elbows that help bench press off the chest so you can handle overload.

items.name: Squat / bench combo rack
items.description: A competition-style rack whose hooks adjust for both squats and bench press, with spotter catches and room for a bench.
items.buying_tips: Found in powerlifting gyms and meets.
items.safety: Set spotter catches every time.

items.name: Wide chest press machine
items.description: Plate-loaded press with wide-set handles and an outward arc that keeps more stretch on the chest.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.buying_tips: Good second chest press if you already own a standard one; feels closer to a fly-press hybrid.
items.safety: Do not let the handles drift behind the shoulders at the bottom.

items.name: Lat pulldown machine
items.description: A seated station with thigh pads and an overhead pulley for pulling a bar down to the chest. The main way to train vertical pulling without doing pull-ups.
items.weight_options: Stack 80–130 kg (180–300 lb); home versions often plate loaded
items.adjustability: Adjustable knee pad; seat height on most.
items.buying_tips: Check the knee pad locks you down and that the stack is heavy enough as you get stronger.

items.name: Seated cable row
items.description: A low pulley with a bench and foot plate for seated horizontal rows. Found as a standalone station or as part of a lat/row combo.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some have adjustable foot plates or a chest pad.
items.buying_tips: Long rails need more floor length than people expect; measure first.

items.name: T-bar row
items.description: Standing row on a pivoting bar anchored at one end and loaded with plates at the other, using a close or wide handle; a landmine is the home substitute.
items.buying_tips: A landmine plus a V-handle covers most of what a dedicated T-bar station does.
items.safety: Brace hard; the standing version loads the lower back.

items.name: Pull-up bar
items.description: A horizontal bar mounted overhead to hang from. The key tool for pull-ups, chin-ups, hanging core work and levers.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some have multiple grip positions (wide, neutral, angled).
items.buying_tips: Pick a bar that is rated well above your body weight and leaves room for your knees and head.
items.safety: Check fixings and load rating before every session if the bar is not permanently mounted.

items.name: Assisted pull-up / dip machine
items.description: Machine with a knee platform that counterweights your body so you can do pull-ups, chin-ups and dips with less than full bodyweight.
items.adjustability: Assistance level via stack pin; platform or knee pad.
items.buying_tips: More assistance = more weight on the stack; it works backwards from other machines.
items.safety: Step off the platform carefully; it moves up when unloaded.

items.name: Back extension / Roman chair
items.description: A 45-degree bench with hip pads and ankle rollers for back extensions, glute-focused extensions and side bends.
items.weight_options: Add plates, dumbbells or bands for load
items.buying_tips: Make sure the hip pad adjusts so the top of it sits just below your hip crease.

items.name: Reverse hyper
items.description: A high pad you lie face-down on while swinging a weighted pendulum (or strap) back behind you with the legs. Trains glutes and lower back with traction on the spine.
items.adjustability: Strap or roller; some have rack-mount versions.
items.buying_tips: Pendulum models are smoother than fixed-arm versions; check the pad height suits your leg length.
items.safety: Do not let the pendulum swing you; control the return.

items.name: Chest-supported row machine
items.description: Seated row with a chest pad and lever handles you pull back; selectorised or plate loaded, with multiple grip options.
items.adjustability: Chest pad and seat height adjust; multiple handles.
items.buying_tips: Look for both neutral and wide handles so you can bias lats or upper back.
items.safety: Keep the chest on the pad and avoid yanking with the lower back.

items.name: Doorway pull-up bar
items.description: A bar that hooks over or wedges inside a door frame with no drilling. Good for strict pull-ups, chin-ups and hangs.
items.weight_options: Fits frames ~60–90 cm wide; rated ~100–150 kg
items.buying_tips: Measure your door frame and moulding depth first; leverage-style bars are sturdier than pure pressure ones.
items.safety: No kipping or muscle-ups on doorway bars; they can pop out.
items.keywords: doorway pull up bar door frame chin up

items.name: Landmine handle
items.description: Handles that fit over the end of a landmine barbell: V-grip for T-bar rows or wide Viking press handles.
items.buying_tips: Rubber-coated handles are comfortable; check sleeve diameter.
items.keywords: landmine handle viking press t bar handle

items.name: Lat pulldown / low row combo
items.description: One stack serving both a high pulley with knee pads for pulldowns and a low pulley with foot plate for rows. The standard home back station.
items.weight_options: Stack 90–110 kg (200–250 lb), or plate loaded
items.adjustability: Adjustable knee pad and seat; swap between pulleys.
items.buying_tips: Plate-loaded versions are cheaper and never run out of weight; stack versions change load faster.

items.name: Rack lat / low row attachment
items.description: A pulley system bolted onto a power rack (or the back of a bench) with a plate horn and seat or foot plate, adding pulldowns, low rows and pushdowns without a separate machine.
items.adjustability: Usually high and low pulleys; some add an adjustable seat.
items.buying_tips: Match the hole spacing and tube size to your rack brand.
items.safety: Make sure the rack is bolted down or heavy enough not to tip.

items.name: Wall / ceiling-mounted pull-up bar
items.description: A bar bolted into wall studs, masonry or ceiling joists. Rigid enough for kipping, muscle-ups and lever work.
items.weight_options: Rated ~150–300 kg; stand-off 50–80 cm from the wall
items.buying_tips: Install into solid masonry or two joists, and leave at least 60 cm overhead clearance.
items.safety: Check bolts regularly and never install into plasterboard alone.
items.keywords: wall mounted ceiling pull up bar

items.name: 90-degree back extension bench
items.description: A flat (horizontal) back extension bench where the torso hangs straight down, giving the hardest top position compared with the 45-degree version.
items.buying_tips: Less common for homes; a GHD does the same plus more.

items.name: Back extension machine
items.description: Seated selectorised machine where you push a pad backward with your upper back to extend the spine against a stack, unlike a Roman chair.
items.adjustability: Seat height and start-angle adjust; foot plate.
items.buying_tips: A combo ab/back unit saves space if you want both movements.
items.safety: Move slowly through a comfortable range; don't fling into extension.

items.name: Chest-supported T-bar row
items.description: Plate-loaded T-bar row where you lie face down on an inclined pad, taking the lower back out of the movement.
items.adjustability: Foot platform or pad height adjust; wide and neutral grips.
items.buying_tips: Several home-gym brands make compact versions; check the pad height fits your torso length.
items.safety: Keep the chin clear of the pad top when rowing.
items.keywords: chest supported t bar incline row

items.name: D.Y. row machine
items.description: Plate-loaded row whose arms follow the underhand, elbows-to-hips path made famous by Dorian Yates, biasing the lats.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.buying_tips: Specialist piece; mostly found in Hammer Strength-equipped gyms.
items.safety: Pull toward the hips, not the chest, to keep the shoulders happy.

items.name: Deadlift machine
items.description: Plate-loaded lever machine you stand in and lift with handles, mimicking a deadlift or trap-bar pull on a fixed arc.
items.adjustability: Handle height or start pins adjust.
items.buying_tips: A trap bar is cheaper and nearly as versatile.
items.safety: Brace as for a barbell deadlift; the machine doesn't hold your back.

items.name: High flat / row bench
items.description: A tall flat bench that lets you lie face down and row a barbell or dumbbells without hitting the floor.
items.buying_tips: Plyo boxes or a flat bench on blocks can stand in.
items.safety: Get on and off carefully; it is high and narrow.
items.keywords: seal row bench high bench row bench

items.name: High row machine
items.description: Seated machine pulling handles down and back from above, between a pulldown and a row, usually plate loaded with independent arms.
items.adjustability: Seat height and thigh pad adjust.
items.buying_tips: Pairs well with a low row if you want both lat and upper-back angles.
items.safety: Lock your thighs under the pad before loading heavy.

items.name: Low row machine
items.description: Seated machine with handles pulled from low in front toward the hips, emphasising the lats.
items.adjustability: Seat height and chest pad adjust.
items.buying_tips: Check the chest pad stops you from leaning back to cheat.
items.safety: Keep the spine neutral on the stretch.

items.name: Lumbar extension machine
items.description: Clinical-style machine that locks the pelvis with thigh and foot restraints so only the lumbar spine extends; used in rehab and strength testing.
items.buying_tips: Mostly found in physio and specialist clinics; ask a trained operator for setup.
items.safety: Set range limits to a pain-free zone before loading.

items.name: Plate-loaded pulldown machine
items.description: Seated pulldown with independent lever arms rather than a cable and bar, usually plate loaded, letting each side pull on its own arc.
items.adjustability: Seat height and thigh pad adjust.
items.buying_tips: Different from a cable lat pulldown: no bar to clear your head and a fixed arc; nice for single-arm work.
items.safety: Secure thighs before loading.

items.name: Plate-loaded row machine
items.description: Chest-supported row with independent plate-loaded lever arms for heavy unilateral or bilateral rowing.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; chest pad sometimes adjusts.
items.buying_tips: Independent arms let you fix side-to-side imbalances.
items.safety: Keep the chest pressed into the pad on the final reps.

items.name: Pulling blocks
items.description: Stackable foam or wooden blocks that raise the plates to a set height for block pulls and hang-position Olympic lifts.
items.buying_tips: Foam blocks are quieter and safer to drop onto than wood.
items.keywords: blocks pulling blocks block pull deficit

items.name: Pullover machine
items.description: Seated machine where your elbows push a pad or bar in an arc from overhead down to the torso, isolating the lats without the biceps.
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; foot lever to bring the bar into start position.
items.buying_tips: Classic Nautilus design; check the shoulder pivot lines up with yours.
items.safety: Use the foot assist to get into and out of the stretch.

items.name: Shrug machine
items.description: Dedicated machine with handles or shoulder pads for heavy trap shrugs, often plate loaded and doubling as a standing calf raise.
items.weight_options: Holds ~200 kg+ of plates or ~150 kg stack
items.adjustability: Handle height or pad height adjust.
items.buying_tips: A trap bar does the same job if space is tight.
items.safety: Keep the neck neutral; don't roll the shoulders.

items.name: Shoulder press machine
items.description: Seated machine pressing handles overhead on a guided path; selectorised in most gyms, plate-loaded and home-multi versions exist.
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; neutral and wide grips.
items.buying_tips: Look for a seat that adjusts low enough for tall users to get a full range.
items.safety: Don't arch the low back off the pad.

items.name: Lateral raise machine
items.description: Seated or standing machine where pads on the upper arms lift sideways to isolate the side delts.
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; some have handle arms.
items.buying_tips: Check that the pivot lines up with your shoulder joint; badly sized ones pinch.
items.safety: Lead with elbows and stop around shoulder height.

items.name: Rear delt machine
items.description: Seated machine (often a reversed pec deck) where you push handles back and out to train the rear delts.
items.adjustability: Seat height and arm start position adjust.
items.buying_tips: Most pec decks convert to this; a dedicated one is rarely needed.
items.safety: Keep a slight elbow bend and don't shrug.

items.name: Landmine attachment
items.description: A pivoting sleeve that holds one end of a barbell on the floor or a rack. For angled presses, rows, rotations and squats.
items.buying_tips: A rack-mounted landmine saves floor; a corner and a towel works as a stand-in.

items.name: Shrug / upright row machine
items.description: Standing machine with handles that travel vertically for upright rows and shrugs; selectorised or plate loaded.
items.buying_tips: Fairly uncommon; a cable station does both movements too.
items.safety: Use a wider grip on upright rows to spare the shoulders.

items.name: Therapy band
items.description: A flat, light latex sheet band used for rehab, rotator-cuff work and warm-ups.
items.adjustability: Cut to length; tie into loops.
items.buying_tips: Rolls are cheaper than precut lengths.
items.safety: Latex allergy? Choose a latex-free band.

items.name: Wrist weights
items.description: Light strap-on wrist weights for shadowboxing, walking and arm-raise circuits.
items.buying_tips: Keep them light, ~0.5–1 kg, for striking work.
items.safety: Do not snap punches to full lock with added weight.

items.name: Jammer press
items.description: Standing plate-loaded machine with long angled lever arms you drive up and forward from the shoulders, used for athletic pushing power.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.adjustability: Handle heights fixed; some have multiple grips.
items.buying_tips: Two landmines with handles are the budget version.
items.safety: Drive from the legs and keep a braced trunk.

items.name: Jerk blocks
items.description: Paired tall blocks at shoulder height. You jerk from them and can drop the bar back onto them safely.
items.buying_tips: Weightlifting-club equipment.

items.name: Plate-loaded shoulder press
items.description: Overhead press with independent plate-loaded arms that converge slightly as you press.
items.weight_options: Holds ~100–200 kg of plates per arm
items.buying_tips: Iso-lateral arms let you press one side at a time without a twist.
items.safety: Keep the ribs down and back on the pad.

items.name: Utility / shoulder press bench
items.description: A short fixed bench with an upright back (near 90 degrees) for seated dumbbell or barbell presses and curls.
items.buying_tips: An adjustable bench usually covers this at home.
items.keywords: utility bench shoulder press seat 90 degree

items.name: EZ curl bar
items.description: A short bar with zig-zag bends that let wrists sit at an angle. Easier on wrists for curls, skull crushers and upright rows.
items.weight_options: 7–12 kg; 1.2–1.3 m; Olympic or standard sleeves
items.buying_tips: Olympic-sleeve EZ bars share plates with your barbell; "super curl" bars have a deeper bend.

items.name: Preacher curl bench
items.description: A seat with an angled arm pad that pins the upper arms for strict curls.
items.buying_tips: Some adjustable benches have a preacher attachment.
items.safety: Don't let the bar crash at the bottom; control the stretch.

items.name: Bicep curl machine
items.description: Seated machine with a preacher-style arm pad and a cam-driven handle for isolated biceps curls.
items.adjustability: Seat height adjust; one- or two-arm handles.
items.buying_tips: If space is tight a preacher bench with an EZ bar covers most of this.
items.safety: Don't let the arms snap straight at the bottom.

items.name: Tricep extension machine
items.description: Seated machine with arm pads where you extend the elbows against a cam to isolate the triceps.
items.buying_tips: Combo biceps/triceps machines are a good space saver at home.
items.safety: Keep the elbows on the pad.

items.name: Dip station / parallel bars
items.description: A standing frame with two parallel handles at about hip height or higher for dips, support holds and leg raises.
items.weight_options: Handles ~50–60 cm apart, user weight ratings 120–180 kg
items.adjustability: Many have adjustable height and width.
items.buying_tips: Heavier, wider bases wobble less; tapered handles let you fit different shoulder widths.
items.safety: Do not let the shoulders roll forward at the bottom of a dip.

items.name: Wrist roller
items.description: A handle with a rope and a plate hanging from it; rolling the rope up and down works the forearms.
items.buying_tips: A thick handle and a long rope give more work per rep.
items.safety: Keep shoulders down; don't drop the weight fast.

items.name: Hand grippers
items.description: Spring-loaded handles you squeeze shut to train crushing grip strength.
items.adjustability: Fixed per gripper; buy several levels.
items.buying_tips: A set of 3–4 levels lets you progress; quality knurled grippers last longer.

items.name: Thick bar grips
items.description: Rubber sleeves that slip over a bar or dumbbell handle to make it thicker and harder to grip.
items.buying_tips: Two sizes cover most uses.

items.name: Finger extensor bands
items.description: Small loops or sleeves you open your fingers against, to balance gripping work and protect elbows.
items.buying_tips: A rubber band works; dedicated bands give more range.

items.name: Flex bar
items.description: A flexible rubber bar you twist and bend to rehab tennis and golfer's elbow.
items.buying_tips: Pick the grade a physio suggests; red or green suits most.

items.name: Grip ball
items.description: A squeezable rubber ball or putty for light grip work and hand rehab.
items.buying_tips: Good for rehab and endurance; not for max grip.

items.name: Gyro wrist ball
items.description: A hand-held gyroscope you spin up with wrist circles, training forearm endurance.
items.buying_tips: Better for endurance and rehab than strength.

items.name: Rice bucket
items.description: A bucket of dry rice you dig, open and twist your hands in to train fingers, wrists and forearms.
items.buying_tips: Any deep bucket and 10 kg of rice works.

items.name: Adjustable hand gripper
items.description: A gripper with a dial that sets the spring tension, so one tool covers many levels.
items.buying_tips: Fine for general grip; serious grip trainers prefer fixed grippers.

items.name: Floor dip bars
items.description: Two separate free-standing bars or a low parallel frame for dips, L-sits, inverted rows and push-ups.
items.adjustability: Width set by where you place them.
items.buying_tips: Heavier bars resist tipping; a cross-brace is more stable for dips.
items.safety: Keep both bars square to each other.

items.name: Grip balls for pull-ups
items.description: Balls or holds hung from a bar to make pull-ups and hangs much harder on the grip.
items.buying_tips: Two sizes give progression.

items.name: Hangboard
items.description: A wall-mounted board with edges and pockets for finger strength, dead hangs and climbing training.
items.buying_tips: Mount above a door frame or on a stud-backed board.
items.safety: Build up slowly; finger tendons adapt slower than muscles.

items.name: Leverage bar
items.description: A handle with weight at one end you lever up and down to train wrist radial and ulnar deviation.
items.weight_options: Handle plus plates; a sledgehammer works
items.adjustability: Slide your hand to change leverage.
items.buying_tips: A loadable dumbbell handle with weight on one end works.
items.safety: Move slowly; don't let it crash into the wrist.

items.name: Biceps / triceps combo machine
items.description: Single-stack machine that switches between a preacher curl and a triceps extension by flipping the arm or handle.
items.adjustability: Seat height; arm converts between curl and extension.
items.buying_tips: Popular in home and hotel gyms; check the changeover is quick.
items.safety: Recheck pin and arm position after switching.

items.name: Pinch block
items.description: A block you pinch between thumb and fingers with weight hung below, for pinch grip strength.
items.adjustability: Load via a loading pin or strap.
items.buying_tips: Pinching two smooth plates or a hex dumbbell head works too.

items.name: Rolling handle
items.description: A spinning handle that hangs weight beneath it, making one-hand holds and deadlifts much harder.
items.buying_tips: Clip onto a loading pin or cable stack.

items.name: Triceps / hammer bar
items.description: A rectangular bar with two parallel neutral-grip handles inside a frame. Used for hammer curls, neutral-grip extensions and close presses.
items.buying_tips: Olympic sleeves and a 1.5 inch handle are the common spec.
items.keywords: tricep bar hammer curl bar neutral

items.name: Fixed-weight barbells
items.description: Pre-loaded short barbells (straight or EZ) with welded or bolted plates, usually on a rack in commercial gyms. Grab-and-go for curls, extensions and rows.
items.weight_options: 10–50 kg in 2.5–5 kg steps; straight and EZ versions
items.buying_tips: For home, a few fixed EZ bars are a space-saving middle ground.
items.keywords: fixed barbell pro style preloaded straight ez

items.name: Grip machine
items.description: Plate-loaded lever you squeeze with the hand to train crushing grip, sometimes with pinch or wrist attachments.
items.buying_tips: Hand grippers are far cheaper; this suits gyms coaching climbers or strongmen.
items.safety: Release slowly to protect the fingers.

items.name: Overhead triceps extension machine
items.description: Seated machine where the arms extend from behind the head, stretching the long head of the triceps under load.
items.buying_tips: Newer machine type; check the elbow pivot lines up with yours.
items.safety: Start light; the stretch position loads the elbow heavily.

items.name: Plate-loaded curl machine
items.description: Plate-loaded biceps machine, preacher or standing style, with independent lever arms.
items.buying_tips: Cheaper than selectorised but plate changes slow down drop sets.
items.safety: Lower under control; the lever can drop fast.

items.name: Seated dip machine
items.description: Seated machine where you push handles down beside the hips, mimicking a dip with the body supported.
items.buying_tips: Good for loading the dip pattern heavily without a dip belt.
items.safety: Keep the shoulders down and back at the bottom.

items.name: Swiss / multi-grip bar
items.description: A barbell frame with several neutral and angled grips. Easier on shoulders and elbows for presses, rows and curls.
items.buying_tips: Angled grips feel better than straight neutral ones for most; check the bar fits your J-cups.
items.keywords: football bar swiss bar multi grip neutral

items.name: Wrist / forearm machine
items.description: Machine with a rotating handle or roller for loaded wrist flexion, extension and roll-ups.
items.weight_options: Plate peg or small stack ~20–60 kg
items.buying_tips: A wrist roller or cable with a short bar does nearly the same job.
items.safety: Use controlled reps; wrist tendons dislike jerks.

items.name: Squat rack / power rack
items.description: A four-post cage with adjustable J-hooks and safety bars, letting you squat, bench and press heavy alone.
items.adjustability: Hole spacing for J-cups and safeties.
items.buying_tips: Check ceiling height, depth, hole spacing (Westside spacing near bench height) and attachment ecosystem.
items.safety: Set safety bars just below the bottom of every rep.

items.name: Leg press
items.description: Seated angled sled you push up rails with the feet; the gym standard, usually plate loaded at about 45 degrees. Feet low on the plate also gives a leg-press calf raise.
items.adjustability: Back-pad angle and safety stops adjust.
items.buying_tips: Check the empty sled weight so you can log loads accurately.
items.safety: Never lock the knees out under load and always set the safety stops.

items.name: Hack squat machine
items.description: Angled sled with shoulder pads; you squat down and up along fixed rails with back supported, very quad focused.
items.adjustability: Foot platform angle on some; safety stops.
items.buying_tips: Check the platform angle; a steeper one shifts load to the quads.
items.safety: Release the safety handles fully before descending and re-engage after.

items.name: Leg extension machine
items.description: Seated machine with a shin pad you kick up to straighten the knees, isolating the quads.
items.adjustability: Back pad, shin pad and start angle adjust.
items.buying_tips: Line the knee joint up with the machine's pivot; look for a range-limiter.
items.safety: Avoid snapping into lockout.

items.name: Lying leg curl machine
items.description: Machine where you lie face down and curl a pad toward your glutes to train the hamstrings.
items.buying_tips: Angled benches (hips higher) feel better than flat ones.
items.safety: Keep hips down on the pad.

items.name: Seated leg curl machine
items.description: Seated machine with a thigh hold-down where you pull a pad down and back to curl the knees; trains hamstrings in a lengthened position.
items.adjustability: Back pad, thigh pad and ankle pad adjust.
items.buying_tips: Many coaches prefer it to the lying curl for hamstring growth.
items.safety: Lock the thigh pad down firmly before starting.

items.name: Standing calf raise machine
items.description: Machine with shoulder pads and a toe block for standing calf raises with heavy load.
items.buying_tips: A leg press or Smith machine with a block covers most needs.
items.safety: Don't bounce out of the bottom stretch.

items.name: Seated calf raise machine
items.description: Seated machine with a knee pad pressing down on the thighs, training the soleus with bent-knee calf raises; usually plate loaded.
items.buying_tips: Compact home versions exist and are inexpensive.
items.safety: Release the safety lever slowly.

items.name: Hip thrust machine
items.description: Machine with a back pad and belt or lever pad over the hips so you can hip-thrust heavy without rolling a barbell on.
items.adjustability: Back pad height and belt adjust.
items.buying_tips: Look for quick in-and-out; belt systems are faster than barbell setups.
items.safety: Keep the chin tucked and stop at full hip extension.

items.name: Glute kickback machine
items.description: Kneeling or standing machine where you push one leg back against a foot plate or pad to train glute hip extension.
items.adjustability: Chest pad and foot plate adjust.
items.buying_tips: A cable with an ankle strap is a cheaper alternative.
items.safety: Don't arch the lower back to finish.

items.name: Hip abductor / adductor machine
items.description: Seated machine with leg pads you push apart (abduction) or squeeze together (adduction) to train the outer glutes and inner thighs.
items.adjustability: Start-width adjust; converts between in and out.
items.buying_tips: Dual units save space; check the changeover is quick.
items.safety: Set a start width within your comfortable range.

items.name: Pendulum / belt squat machine
items.description: Plate-loaded squat where shoulder pads ride on a swinging pendulum arm, giving a deep, quad-heavy squat with a smooth strength curve. Belt squat machines are now listed separately.
items.adjustability: Foot platform and pad adjust; safety stops.
items.buying_tips: Getting more common; feels lighter than a hack squat at the same plate load.
items.safety: Set the depth stop for your mobility.

items.name: Glute-ham developer (GHD)
items.description: A bench with a hip pad and a foot plate with ankle rollers. Used for glute-ham raises, GHD sit-ups, back and hip extensions, and assisted Nordics.
items.weight_options: Add plates or bands for load
items.adjustability: Adjustable foot plate distance and pad height.
items.buying_tips: A good GHD has a large footplate adjustment range and a stable, heavy base.
items.safety: Build up to GHD sit-ups slowly; they are very hard on the hip flexors at first.

items.name: Plyo box
items.description: A sturdy box for box jumps, step-ups and depth drops. Wooden 3-in-1 boxes give three heights by flipping.
items.buying_tips: Check it's stable on every face; steel boxes are sturdier but hurt more on a miss.
items.safety: Step down rather than jumping down for reps.

items.name: Push / pull sled
items.description: A weighted sled with push uprights you drive across turf, and a hook to drag with a harness or rope. Huge leg work without eccentric soreness.
items.weight_options: Sled 20–45 kg empty; load with plates
items.adjustability: High and low push handles on most.
items.buying_tips: Needs turf or a smooth outdoor surface; check runners suit your floor.

items.name: Aerobic step
items.description: A low adjustable platform with risers for step-ups, step aerobics, calf raises and decline or incline push-ups.
items.adjustability: Add or remove risers to change height.
items.buying_tips: A non-slip top and locking risers matter most.
items.safety: Place the step on a flat, non-slip floor.

items.name: Ankle weights
items.description: Strap-on weights for the ankles that add load to leg raises, kickbacks and hip work.
items.weight_options: ~0.5–5 kg per ankle; some adjustable with pockets
items.adjustability: Adjustable pocket versions add weight in small steps.
items.buying_tips: Adjustable pocket types last longer as you get stronger.
items.safety: Avoid running or jumping in ankle weights; it stresses the knees and hips.

items.name: Bar pad
items.description: A foam sleeve that wraps a barbell to cushion the hips in hip thrusts and glute bridges.
items.buying_tips: Thick, dense foam is best; avoid using it for squats.
items.safety: Don't use a pad for back squats; it makes the bar roll.
items.keywords: bar pad hip thrust pad manta ray

items.name: Bench leg attachment
items.description: A leg extension and leg curl arm that bolts onto a home bench and takes plates.
items.buying_tips: Check it fits your bench brand; many are model-specific.
items.keywords: leg developer extension curl attachment bench

items.name: Fabric hip circle
items.description: A wide woven-fabric loop worn above the knees. Stiffer than a latex mini band and does not roll up.
items.buying_tips: Pick the right size for your thigh circumference; elastic weave grips best.

items.name: Mini band
items.description: A short thin latex loop worn around the thighs or ankles for glute activation, lateral walks and hip work.
items.adjustability: Change band or move it lower for more tension.
items.buying_tips: Latex mini bands are cheap but can roll; fabric versions stay put.
items.keywords: mini band booty band glute loop

items.name: Nordic curl strap
items.description: A padded ankle strap that anchors under a door, around a bench or to the floor so you can do Nordic curls without a partner.
items.buying_tips: Check the anchor is rated for your bodyweight; door anchors need a solid door.
items.safety: Use a thick pad under the knees.

items.name: Squat wedge / slant board
items.description: An angled wedge or slant board that raises the heels for deeper, more quad-focused squats and calf stretching.
items.buying_tips: A pair of small plates under the heels works as a stand-in.
items.keywords: slant board squat wedge heel elevation

items.name: Folding wall rack
items.description: A wall-mounted rack that swings out for training and folds flat against the wall afterwards. Ideal for garages.
items.buying_tips: Needs solid studs or masonry for mounting; check it folds past your car mirror.
items.safety: Must be bolted into structural framing.
items.keywords: folding rack wall mount garage pr-4100

items.name: Half rack
items.description: Two uprights with J-cups and short spotter arms, often with a pull-up bar. Takes less depth than a full cage.
items.buying_tips: Spotter arms must be long enough to catch the bar where you bench and squat.
items.safety: Set spotter arms for every heavy set.

items.name: Hip thrust bench
items.description: A low bench or box with a back pad at the right height for hip thrusts, often with band pegs or a foot plate.
items.buying_tips: A flat bench placed against a wall works almost as well.
items.safety: Brace the bench so it cannot slide back.
items.keywords: hip thrust bench glute box thruster

items.name: J-cups / J-hooks
items.description: The hooks that hang on rack uprights to hold the bar. Usually included with a rack; extra pairs or roller versions are common upgrades.
items.buying_tips: Plastic-lined (UHMW) hooks protect bar knurling.
items.safety: Seat both hooks fully before loading.
items.keywords: j hooks j cups rack hooks

items.name: Leg extension / curl combo
items.description: Home-gym unit (standalone or a bench attachment) that does both leg extensions and leg curls, plate loaded or selectorised.
items.weight_options: Plate post ~100 kg capacity or ~70 kg stack
items.adjustability: Pad positions adjust; seated or lying curl depending on model.
items.buying_tips: Bench attachments are cheap but the pivot rarely lines up well; standalone units feel better.
items.safety: Make sure the bench is rated for the load you'll use.
items.keywords: leg extension leg curl home combo

items.name: Leg press / hack squat combo
items.description: Home-gym plate-loaded sled that converts between a 45-degree leg press and a hack squat by swapping the seat and shoulder pads.
items.buying_tips: The best value way to get a leg press at home; check conversion time and empty sled weight.
items.safety: Engage the safety catches before every set.
items.keywords: leg press hack squat combo home

items.name: Leverage squat machine
items.description: Plate-loaded lever arm with shoulder pads that you squat or lunge under while standing on a platform; a Smith-like squat with a curved path, common in home gyms.
items.adjustability: Pad height and safety stops adjust.
items.buying_tips: Many home versions double as a calf raise and shrug station.
items.safety: Keep feet forward enough that knees stay comfortable at the bottom.
items.keywords: lever squat super squat power squat

items.name: Nordic curl bench
items.description: A padded kneeling bench with fixed ankle hooks for Nordic hamstring curls; some angle or add a reverse-Nordic setting.
items.adjustability: Some adjust the ankle hooks and angle.
items.buying_tips: Look for thick knee padding and an incline option to progress gradually.
items.safety: Start with partial range; Nordics cause major soreness at first.

items.name: Sissy squat bench
items.description: A low frame with a calf pad and foot plate that locks the lower legs so you can lean back into a sissy squat for intense quad work.
items.buying_tips: Look for a wide base and adjustable roller so it fits your shin length.
items.safety: Build up slowly; knees take a lot of stress.

items.name: Sissy squat machine
items.description: Small frame with a padded foot lock and calf pad that lets you lean back into a sissy squat safely; load with a plate held to the chest.
items.weight_options: Bodyweight; hold a plate to load
items.adjustability: Foot and calf pad height adjust.
items.buying_tips: Cheap and compact; check the calf pad height suits your shin length.
items.safety: Progress slowly; it loads the knee hard.

items.name: Spotter arms / safety straps
items.description: Safety bars, pins, arms or nylon straps that catch a failed barbell. Make heavy squats and bench safe alone.
items.buying_tips: Straps are quieter and kinder to bars; flip-down arms suit half racks and stands.
items.safety: Set them every set just below your lowest bar position.
items.keywords: spotter arms safety straps pins safeties

items.name: Squat stands
items.description: Two independent or base-linked uprights with J-cups. The cheapest and smallest way to rack a barbell.
items.buying_tips: Base-linked stands are more stable; independent stands need careful spacing.
items.safety: Add spotter arms or straps, or bench and squat with a spotter.

items.name: Tibia raise machine
items.description: Seated or standing device with a padded foot hook you load with plates to train the tibialis by pulling the toes up.
items.adjustability: Foot pad position adjust on some.
items.buying_tips: A cheap tib bar or band does most of the job; machines suit gyms.
items.safety: Start light; the shins fatigue fast.

items.name: Belt squat machine
items.description: Machine that loads a belt round your hips so you can squat, march or lunge with zero load on the spine; plate-loaded lever or cable-driven.
items.adjustability: Belt chain length adjust; handles for balance.
items.buying_tips: Home lifters can approximate with a dip belt between two boxes or a landmine belt-squat attachment.
items.safety: Adjust chain length so you start standing tall with the load off the stops.

items.name: Buffalo bar
items.description: A barbell with a gentle curve through the middle that wraps around the back. Easier on the shoulders for back squats and good mornings.
items.buying_tips: Mainly a powerlifting accessory; check it fits your rack.

items.name: Calibrated steel plates
items.description: Thin, precisely weighed steel plates used in powerlifting meets. Fit more weight on the bar and are accurate to a few grams.
items.buying_tips: Only needed for meet-style heavy training or very heavy lifters running out of sleeve.
items.safety: Do not drop; they are not designed for it.

items.name: Cambered bar
items.description: A barbell whose ends drop down several inches below the shaft, so the weight swings and sits lower. Used for squats, good mornings and bench press.
items.buying_tips: Rare in home gyms; check drop depth and that it fits your rack.
items.safety: The swinging plates demand control; use safeties.

items.name: Deadlift bar
items.description: A longer, thinner (27 mm), whippier 20 kg bar that bends before the plates leave the floor, letting you pull more weight.
items.buying_tips: Only worth it for competitive powerlifters; don't use it for squats or bench.
items.safety: Not rated for squatting or benching.

items.name: Donkey calf raise machine
items.description: Machine where you bend forward at the hips with a pad on the lower back and raise onto the toes, stretching the calves hard.
items.buying_tips: Rare; a leg press calf raise gives a similar stretch.
items.safety: Keep the back flat under the pad.

items.name: Flywheel (isoinertial) trainer
items.description: A strap wound around a spinning flywheel: you pull to spin it up and then brake it on the way back, giving hard eccentric overload. Used for squats, rows and sport training.
items.weight_options: Swappable flywheels set the inertia (resistance comes from flywheel inertia, not weights)
items.adjustability: Change flywheel discs or cone; harness or handle attaches to the strap.
items.buying_tips: Most used in sport and rehab; portable units exist but the platform type is the most versatile.
items.safety: Learn the timing on light flywheels first; the eccentric is much harder than it feels.

items.name: Hip extension machine
items.description: Selectorised machine (Nautilus Duo Hip & Back style) where you lie or stand and push a roller pad down with the thigh, training glutes and hamstrings through hip extension.
items.adjustability: Back pad and start angle adjust.
items.buying_tips: Mostly in older Nautilus-equipped gyms; a multi-hip covers the same movement.
items.safety: Keep the lower back neutral as the leg drives down.

items.name: Hip flexion machine
items.description: Machine with a thigh pad you lift toward the chest, loading the hip flexors directly; useful for sprinters and kickers.
items.buying_tips: Specialist piece; a multi-hip machine or cable with ankle strap covers it.
items.safety: Avoid arching the back to lift the leg higher.

items.name: Iso-lateral horizontal leg press
items.description: Plate-loaded horizontal leg press with two independent footplates, so each leg can push separately on a curved path.
items.weight_options: Holds ~150–200 kg of plates per side
items.buying_tips: Great for unilateral work without the balance demand of split squats.
items.safety: Load both sides evenly before getting in.

items.name: Kneeling leg curl machine
items.description: Machine where you kneel on one leg and curl the other against a pad, a one-leg-at-a-time hamstring isolation.
items.buying_tips: Mostly in older or European gyms (Gym80, Panatta).
items.safety: Keep hips square; don't twist to finish the rep.

items.name: Monolift
items.description: A rack whose hooks swing away after unracking, so you squat without walking the bar out. Used for very heavy powerlifting squats.
items.buying_tips: Rare outside powerlifting gyms.
items.safety: Needs trained operators or spotters.

items.name: Multi-hip machine
items.description: Standing machine with a rotating lever pad at thigh height that trains hip extension, flexion, abduction and adduction one leg at a time.
items.adjustability: Platform height and lever start angle adjust.
items.buying_tips: One machine covers four hip movements; great for small rehab or PT studios.
items.safety: Raise the platform so your hip joint lines up with the lever's pivot.

items.name: Open trap bar
items.description: A trap bar with one side open, so you can step in and out. Also allows lunges, split squats and longer strides without hitting the frame.
items.adjustability: Dual-height handles; some have rack hooks.
items.buying_tips: More expensive than a closed hex bar; worth it if you want carries and lunges.
items.keywords: open trap bar open hex kabuki rogue tib

items.name: Powerlifting bar
items.description: A stiff 20 kg, 29 mm bar with aggressive knurling and a centre knurl. Built for heavy squats, bench presses and deadlifts with minimal whip.
items.buying_tips: Stiffness and grippy knurl are the point; IPF knurl marks matter for meet prep.

items.name: Rotary calf machine
items.description: Selectorised seated machine where you push a footplate with the balls of your feet on an arc, training the calves with the legs straight.
items.buying_tips: A leg press with feet low on the plate does nearly the same job.
items.safety: Keep the knees soft, not locked.

items.name: Safety squat bar
items.description: A padded yoke bar with forward handles and cambered ends. Lets you squat with sore shoulders and loads the upper back and quads harder.
items.buying_tips: Check camber, pad comfort and whether it fits your rack's J-cups.
items.safety: Rack it carefully; the pad shifts the balance forward.

items.name: Seated leg press machine
items.description: Upright seat with the footplate in front; you push horizontally against a weight stack. Lighter loads than a plate-loaded sled, quick to adjust.
items.adjustability: Seat position and back angle adjust.
items.buying_tips: Common add-on for home multi-gyms; strong lifters may max out the stack.
items.safety: Set the seat so knees don't fold past 90 degrees into the chest.

items.name: Standing hip thrust machine
items.description: You stand facing the machine with a belt or pad at the hips and drive them forward, loading the glutes at end range in an upright position.
items.buying_tips: Quicker to set up than a lying hip thrust; newer and less common.
items.safety: Don't hyperextend the lower back at lockout.

items.name: Standing leg curl machine
items.description: Upright machine where you brace on a thigh pad and curl one leg back against a shin pad.
items.adjustability: Thigh and ankle pad height adjust.
items.buying_tips: Takes less space than a lying curl; good for unilateral work.
items.safety: Keep the standing knee soft and the hips still.

items.name: V-squat machine
items.description: Plate-loaded lever squat: shoulder pads on a pivoting arm with your back facing the frame; deep squatting with less spinal load than a barbell.
items.adjustability: Fixed; some have adjustable shoulder pads.
items.buying_tips: Rarer than a hack squat but feels more natural; worth seeking out.
items.safety: Control the bottom position; the lever accelerates on the way down.

items.name: Vertical leg press
items.description: You lie on your back and press a plate-loaded sled straight up; compact but hard on the lower back if you round.
items.adjustability: Safety stop; seat pad sometimes adjusts.
items.buying_tips: Small footprint makes it popular in home gyms and as a Smith/rack add-on.
items.safety: Keep the hips down on the pad; don't let the sled come too deep.

items.name: Ab / decline sit-up bench
items.description: An angled bench with leg rollers to hook the feet for decline sit-ups and crunches, or handles for reverse leg raises. Usually adjustable in angle.
items.weight_options: Hold a plate or medicine ball for load
items.adjustability: Adjustable decline angle and roller height.
items.buying_tips: Check that the foot rollers fit tall users and the angle adjusts in several steps.

items.name: Ab roller wheel
items.description: A wheel with handles you roll out in front of you while bracing the trunk. A very effective anti-extension core tool.
items.weight_options: Single or double wheel; spring-assisted 'carver' versions exist
items.buying_tips: A wide or double wheel is more stable for beginners; add a knee pad.
items.safety: Stop the rollout before your lower back sags.

items.name: Captain's chair / knee raise station
items.description: An upright frame with a back pad and elbow pads where you support yourself on the forearms and raise your knees or legs.
items.weight_options: Add ankle weights or a dumbbell between the feet
items.adjustability: Fixed; often combined with dip handles.
items.buying_tips: Check the elbow pads are thick and the back pad tall enough for your height.

items.name: Hanging ab straps
items.description: Padded loops that hang from a pull-up bar so you can rest your upper arms in them and do knee and leg raises without grip limiting you.
items.buying_tips: Look for wide padding and metal hooks rather than plastic.
items.safety: Lower your legs under control to avoid swinging.

items.name: Ab crunch machine
items.description: Seated machine with chest pads or handles you curl forward against a stack, loading the abs through a crunch.
items.buying_tips: Pick one where your hips stay put and only the spine flexes.
items.safety: Exhale and curl; don't pull with the arms.

items.name: Rotary torso machine
items.description: Seated machine where you twist the upper body against a stack to train the obliques.
items.buying_tips: Cable woodchops and Pallof presses cover much of this.
items.safety: Rotate slowly through a comfortable range.

items.name: Medicine ball
items.description: A weighted ball for throws, passes, twists and loaded core work; rubber ones bounce back off walls and the floor.
items.weight_options: 1–12 kg (2–25 lb); rubber bouncing or soft
items.buying_tips: 3–5 kg suits most adults for throws; rubber bouncing balls are best for rebounds.
items.safety: Don't slam a bouncing ball; it can fly back at your face.

items.name: Stability / Swiss ball
items.description: A large inflatable ball used for core, balance and supported stretching work.
items.adjustability: Choose by height; firmness by inflation.
items.buying_tips: Anti-burst rated; 65 cm suits most adults 165–185 cm tall.
items.safety: Inflate fully and keep away from sharp objects.

items.name: BOSU ball
items.description: A half-sphere on a flat base for balance, core and plyometric work on either side.
items.buying_tips: Branded ones last longer; compare the base grip.
items.safety: Step on dome-up for balance; flat-side-up is much harder.

items.name: Balance cushion
items.description: A small inflatable disc for balance work or active sitting.
items.buying_tips: Cheap way to add instability to home workouts.

items.name: Knee pad / cushion
items.description: A thick foam pad or cushion for kneeling exercises like ab-wheel rollouts, Nordics and half-kneeling work.
items.buying_tips: Dense foam stays supportive; a folded towel works in a pinch.

items.name: Ab rocker / crunch frame
items.description: A rocking frame or padded lounge chair that supports the head and guides the crunch path. Mainly for beginners.
items.buying_tips: Adds little beyond a floor crunch for most people; useful if neck strain is the issue.

items.name: AbMat
items.description: A curved foam pad placed under the lower back for full-range sit-ups.
items.buying_tips: Add a tailbone pad if you do high-rep sit-ups.

items.name: Balance beam
items.description: A narrow raised or floor beam for balance and gymnastics drills.
items.buying_tips: Folding floor beams store easily.

items.name: Balance board
items.description: A deck on a roller or rocker that moves side to side for surf, ski and skate balance training.
items.buying_tips: Roller boards are harder than rocker boards; start on carpet.
items.safety: Use near a wall and wear a helmet on roller boards early on.

items.name: Balance pad
items.description: A thick, soft foam pad that makes standing exercises less stable.
items.buying_tips: Closed-cell foam doesn't flatten as fast.

items.name: Balance pods
items.description: Small half-domes placed on the floor to step or stand on for balance and agility.
items.buying_tips: Good for rehab and kids' circuits.

items.name: Core sliders
items.description: Low-friction discs placed under hands or feet for body saws, sliding leg curls, lunges and mountain climbers.
items.weight_options: Two-sided (fabric for hard floors, plastic for carpet)
items.buying_tips: Double-sided sliders work on carpet and wood.
items.safety: Keep the floor clean; grit makes sliders stick suddenly.

items.name: Handled medicine ball
items.description: A medicine ball with one or two built-in handles, making it easier to hold for twists, chops, push-ups and kettlebell-style moves.
items.buying_tips: Handles make it unsuitable for slams or wall throws.

items.name: Sit-up bar
items.description: A small floor or under-door anchor that holds your feet down for sit-ups.
items.buying_tips: Suction-based ones slip on rugs; door-mounted are more secure.

items.name: Slackline
items.description: A flat webbing line tensioned between two anchors (trees or a frame) and walked for balance.
items.buying_tips: Starter kits include a training line; protect trees with tree pads.
items.safety: Keep it low and over soft ground.

items.name: Wobble board
items.description: A round board on a half-sphere that tilts in all directions to train ankle stability.
items.adjustability: Some have removable domes for different difficulty.
items.buying_tips: Wooden boards with a grippy top are durable.
items.safety: Start beside a wall or rail.

items.name: Ab / back combo machine
items.description: Single-stack machine that switches between a seated crunch and a seated back extension.
items.adjustability: Converts via seat or lever position.
items.buying_tips: Common in home and hotel gyms; saves a second machine.
items.safety: Check the pin and lever after switching modes.

items.name: Ab coaster
items.description: Curved rail with a sliding knee seat; you hold handles and pull the knees up the rail for a reverse crunch.
items.weight_options: Bodyweight; some add a plate peg
items.adjustability: Some have resistance settings or plate pegs.
items.buying_tips: Mostly a home fitness product; hanging knee raises do similar work for free.
items.safety: Move slowly; don't let momentum swing the seat.

items.name: 4-way neck machine
items.description: Seated machine with a padded head piece that trains neck flexion, extension and side bending against a stack; found in sports and combat gyms.
items.adjustability: Seat height and head-pad position adjust; rotates for each direction.
items.buying_tips: A neck harness and plates are far cheaper.
items.safety: Use very light weights and slow controlled reps.

items.name: Dumbbells
items.description: Hand-held weights with a short handle and a fixed load on each end. The most versatile free weight for presses, rows, curls, lunges and carries.
items.weight_options: 1–50+ kg (2–120 lb) pairs, usually in 1–2.5 kg (2.5–5 lb) steps
items.adjustability: Fixed per dumbbell; a full rack covers the range.
items.buying_tips: Rubber or urethane heads protect floors; knurled steel handles grip better than chrome. Buy pairs in the range you will actually use.
items.safety: Set dumbbells down under control rather than dropping them.

items.name: Olympic barbell
items.description: A 2.2 m, 20 kg steel bar with 50 mm rotating sleeves that take Olympic plates. The base of squats, bench presses, deadlifts and Olympic lifts.
items.weight_options: Bar 20 kg (44 lb), 2.2 m, 28–29 mm shaft; holds 300+ kg
items.buying_tips: A multipurpose 28.5 mm bar with bushings or bearings, dual knurl marks and ~190k PSI tensile strength suits most lifters.
items.safety: Use collars and safeties, and never bench or squat heavy without a spotter or safety arms.

items.name: Weight plates
items.description: Cast-iron or urethane plates with a 50 mm hole that load Olympic bars, trap bars and plate-loaded machines.
items.buying_tips: Machined cast iron is cheapest per kg; urethane or rubber coated is quieter. Buy pairs.
items.safety: Never drop iron plates from height; they crack floors and plates.

items.name: Kettlebells
items.description: Cast-iron balls with a thick handle, with the weight sitting below the grip. Built for swings, cleans, snatches, goblet squats and carries.
items.buying_tips: Single-piece cast iron with a smooth, seamless handle; check the handle width fits two hands for swings.
items.safety: Swing with your hips, not your lower back, and keep a clear space around you.

items.name: Adjustable bench
items.description: A bench whose back pad adjusts from flat to upright (flat/incline). The single most useful bench for home gyms.
items.buying_tips: Check the gap between seat and back pad at incline, the ladder angles and weight rating.

items.name: Cable crossover
items.description: Two tall weight-stack towers joined by a frame, each with a pulley that slides from floor to overhead. The gym standard for cable flys, pushdowns, face pulls and almost any cable exercise.
items.weight_options: Two stacks of ~70–115 kg (150–250 lb) each, usually 1:1 or 2:1 cable ratio
items.adjustability: Pulleys adjust in 15–30 positions; most have a pull-up bar across the top.
items.buying_tips: Check the cable ratio: 2:1 stacks feel half as heavy and travel twice as far, so numbers are not comparable to 1:1 machines.
items.safety: Check cables for fraying and that the pin is fully seated before each set.

items.name: Functional trainer / cable column
items.description: A compact two-stack cable machine with swivelling arms that move up and down a column, letting you pull from any height and angle. The most popular cable unit for home gyms.
items.weight_options: Two 70–100 kg (150–220 lb) stacks, usually 2:1 ratio
items.adjustability: Arms adjust in height (and on some, pivot sideways); usually a top pull-up bar.
items.buying_tips: Look for smooth pulleys, enough cable travel for overhead work (check 2:1 travel length) and fine weight increments.
items.safety: Keep fingers away from the stack and moving pulleys.

items.name: Smith machine
items.description: A barbell fixed in guide rails with hooks you twist to rack it at many heights. Lets you squat, press and lunge without a spotter, and doubles as a fixed bar for inverted rows.
items.weight_options: Bar 7–25 kg (counterbalanced bars feel lighter than their weight)
items.adjustability: Vertical or 5–7° angled rails; adjustable safety stops.
items.buying_tips: Ask what the bar weighs (or its counterbalance) so you can log real loads; linear-bearing rails glide best.
items.safety: Set the safety stops just below your lowest point every time.

items.name: Trap / hex bar
items.description: A hexagonal bar you stand inside, with handles at your sides. Makes deadlifts, shrugs and carries easier on the lower back.
items.weight_options: 20–30 kg; most have low and high handles
items.buying_tips: Look for raised (high) handles and 60+ cm inside width; check sleeve length if you lift heavy.

items.name: Resistance bands
items.description: Elastic bands for adding resistance or assistance to almost any movement. The general family includes loop, tube, mini and therapy bands.
items.weight_options: Usually sold in colour-coded sets from ~2 kg to 80+ kg of tension
items.adjustability: Change resistance by switching bands, doubling up or moving your stance.
items.buying_tips: A set of 4–5 loop bands plus a door anchor covers most home needs.
items.safety: Check bands for nicks or tears and replace them before they snap.

items.name: Suspension trainer (TRX)
items.description: Two adjustable nylon straps with handles and foot cradles, anchored overhead. You change difficulty by changing your body angle.
items.weight_options: Straps adjust ~1.3–2.0 m, anchor rated 150+ kg
items.adjustability: Single-point anchor; strap length adjusts quickly.
items.buying_tips: Look for a door anchor and extension strap in the box; cheap copies often have weak buckles.
items.safety: Always test the anchor with a bodyweight pull before leaning back.

items.name: Battle ropes
items.description: Heavy, thick ropes anchored at the middle that you whip in waves and slams for upper-body conditioning.
items.adjustability: Change length or thickness to adjust difficulty.
items.buying_tips: Poly-dacron ropes shed less than manila; 38 mm x 12 m suits most people.

items.name: Punching bag
items.description: A heavy hanging bag for punching and kicking; long (banana) bags suit kicks and knees.
items.adjustability: Fixed; mount height adjustable by chain.
items.buying_tips: Buy a bag about half your body weight and a ceiling mount or stand rated for it.
items.safety: Always wrap hands and wear gloves.

items.name: Sandbag
items.description: A fillable bag of sand or pellets; handled versions suit cleans and presses, round strongman bags suit carries and loads.
items.adjustability: Adjust with filler bags; handles vary by model.
items.buying_tips: Pick a tough outer shell with inner filler bags; strongman bags have no handles.
items.safety: Contain the filler in sealed inner bags so it doesn't burst.

items.name: Home multi-gym
items.description: One frame with a weight stack and several stations: chest press, pec fly, lat pulldown, low row, leg extension and curl. Covers the basics in a small space.
items.adjustability: Adjustable seat, arms and pulleys; stations vary by model.
items.buying_tips: Look for a stack heavy enough for leg work and a low pulley; cheaper units have small stacks and jerky cables.

items.name: Weighted vest
items.description: A vest holding sand, iron bars or plates that adds load to bodyweight moves, walks and runs.
items.weight_options: Fixed 5–20 kg or adjustable vests up to ~40 kg
items.adjustability: Many vests take removable weight blocks or plates.
items.buying_tips: A snug, adjustable fit matters more than maximum weight, especially for running.
items.safety: Start light; extra load raises stress on knees and the lower back.

items.name: Adjustable dumbbells
items.description: A pair of dumbbells whose load changes with a dial, pin or slide selector while sitting in a cradle. Replaces a whole rack in a small space.
items.weight_options: Typically 2–24 kg (5–52.5 lb) or 2.5–41 kg (5–90 lb) per hand
items.adjustability: Dial, pin, slide or twist selector; 1–2.5 kg steps.
items.buying_tips: Check the minimum and maximum weight, step size, length at light settings and whether it tolerates drops (most do not).
items.safety: Never drop selector dumbbells, and make sure the selector has fully locked before lifting.

items.name: Adjustable kettlebell
items.description: A kettlebell whose weight changes by adding plates or using a dial or pin selector. Saves buying a full set.
items.weight_options: Usually 4–18 kg or 12–32 kg; plate-loadable handles up to ~40 kg
items.buying_tips: Shell size at light settings matters for cleans and snatches; check locking mechanism quality.
items.safety: Confirm the selector or plate lock is secure before swinging.

items.name: Band bar
items.description: A short bar that bands clip onto, making band squats, deadlifts, presses and rows feel more like barbell lifts.
items.weight_options: Bar ~100–130 cm, used with bands of 10–100 kg
items.buying_tips: Pick one with a foot plate if you want ground-based lifts.
items.safety: Keep the band centred under your feet.

items.name: Barbell collars
items.description: Clips or clamps that hold plates on the bar sleeves. Stop plates sliding off and keep load even.
items.weight_options: Spring clips, lock-jaw/clip collars, screw or lever competition collars (2.5 kg each)
items.buying_tips: Lock-jaw style is quick and reliable; spring clips loosen with wear.
items.safety: Always use collars on moving or overhead lifts.

items.name: Clubbells / Indian clubs
items.description: Long bottle-shaped weights held at the thin end and swung in circles. Train rotational strength, grip and shoulder mobility.
items.buying_tips: Start very light (Indian clubs or 4–7 kg) to learn patterns; check the handle has a knob so it cannot fly out.
items.safety: Swing only in a clear area with plenty of ceiling height.

items.name: Folding bench
items.description: A flat or adjustable bench that folds flat or stands upright for storage. For small homes.
items.buying_tips: Check weight rating and wobble; cheaper ones flex under heavy pressing.

items.name: Hex dumbbells
items.description: Fixed dumbbells with six-sided rubber or iron heads that do not roll. Stable on the floor for push-ups, renegade rows and burpee complexes.
items.buying_tips: Rubber-coated hex heads are quieter and floor-friendly; check the head is bonded tightly to the handle.
items.safety: Check heads are tight before putting body weight on them in push-up positions.

items.name: Incline bodyweight trainer
items.description: A sliding seat on an adjustable incline rail with cables: you pull or push yourself up the slope, so steeper angles mean more load. Folds flat for storage.
items.weight_options: Load is a share of bodyweight set by the incline
items.adjustability: Incline adjusts in 6–12 levels; some take add-on weight bars.
items.buying_tips: Check the user weight limit and how flat it folds.

items.name: Loading pin pulley (DIY cable)
items.description: A pulley wheel, steel cable and loading pin that clip onto a rack, pull-up bar or wall anchor. The cheapest way to do cable pushdowns, curls and pulldowns at home.
items.adjustability: Clip the pulley at any height on a rack or bar.
items.buying_tips: Pick a steel cable (not nylon cord) and ball-bearing pulleys; buy a long enough cable for overhead extensions.
items.safety: Inspect the cable and clips every session; keep your head out of the line of pull.

items.name: Loop / power band
items.description: A long, closed latex loop (~2 m). Used for assisted pull-ups, mobility, band-resisted lifts and sprints.
items.buying_tips: Buy a set of 3–4 widths; layered latex lasts longer than moulded.
items.safety: Anchor securely and keep bands away from your face.
items.keywords: power band loop super band pull up assist

items.name: Portable digital cable trainer
items.description: A small motor box with one cable that anchors to the floor, a door, a rack or a wall. Gives cable training with app-set resistance anywhere.
items.weight_options: Up to ~25–100 kg (50–220 lb) depending on model
items.adjustability: Anchor at any height; modes for eccentric, isokinetic, chains.
items.buying_tips: Check what the anchor options are and whether the cable is long enough for overhead work.
items.safety: Make sure the anchor is rated above the maximum load.

items.name: Power rod / bow home gym
items.description: A compact home gym that uses bending rods instead of weights, with cables and a sliding bench for presses, rows, curls and leg work.
items.weight_options: Rods 5–200+ kg-equivalent; resistance rises as they bend
items.adjustability: Swap rods to change load; adjustable bench.
items.buying_tips: Rated loads are at full bend, so the real resistance is lower; good for beginners and tight budgets.

items.name: Short Olympic bar
items.description: A 1.5–1.8 m bar with Olympic sleeves for small rooms. Fine for floor and bench work but too short for most standard racks.
items.buying_tips: Check it reaches across the uprights of your rack or bench before buying.

items.name: Spin-lock dumbbell handles
items.description: Threaded dumbbell handles you load with small plates and secure with spin-lock collars. A cheap way to build adjustable dumbbells.
items.weight_options: Handle ~2 kg; sets load to 10–30 kg per hand (1-inch or Olympic 2-inch versions)
items.adjustability: Add or remove plates; slow to change.
items.buying_tips: Olympic-diameter handles let you share plates with your barbell; long handles limit some movements.
items.safety: Re-tighten the spin-lock collars every set; loose plates can slide off.

items.name: Standard 1-inch bar
items.description: A thin, cheap barbell with 25 mm (1-inch) ends that takes standard plates. Common in starter home sets.
items.buying_tips: Fine for light work; upgrade to an Olympic bar once lifts get heavier.
items.safety: The thin bar bends and is not rated for heavy squats or deadlifts.

items.name: Standard 1-inch plates
items.description: Plates with a 25–28 mm hole for standard bars and spin-lock dumbbell handles. Cheap and common in starter sets.
items.buying_tips: They do not fit Olympic bars; buy Olympic plates if you might upgrade.

items.name: Steel mace
items.description: A long steel handle with a weighted ball on one end, swung around the body. Builds rotational strength, grip and shoulder control.
items.buying_tips: A 7 kg mace is plenty to start for most people; length changes leverage more than weight.
items.safety: Needs a lot of overhead and side clearance.

items.name: Tube band with handles
items.description: A rubber tube with a handle at each end, often clip-on so you can stack tubes. Mimics cable work at home.
items.adjustability: Clip on more tubes or step further away.
items.buying_tips: Clip-on sets with ankle straps and a door anchor give the most options.
items.safety: Check the tube where it joins the clip; that is where it fails.

items.name: Bumper plates
items.description: Thick rubber plates all the same diameter, made to be dropped from overhead. Essential for Olympic lifting and CrossFit.
items.buying_tips: Low-bounce virgin rubber or urethane lasts longest; 10 kg bumpers are thick, so check bar sleeve space.
items.safety: Drop only on a platform or rubber floor, and not with an empty bar.

items.name: Competition kettlebell
items.description: Steel kettlebells that are the same size at every weight, with a uniform handle for kettlebell sport. Technique stays identical as weight goes up.
items.buying_tips: Pick a 33–35 mm handle for sport; cheaper "pro-grade" bells may not be true competition spec.

items.name: Digital platform trainer
items.description: A floor platform with motor-driven cables coming up from the base. Ideal for squats, deadlifts, rows and curls with instant load changes and eccentric overload.
items.buying_tips: Only pulls from the floor, so pair with bands or a bar for pulldown-type moves.
items.safety: Stand centred so cables run vertically.

items.name: Dumbbell rack
items.description: Two- or three-tier rack or tree that holds dumbbells or kettlebells off the floor. Keeps weights tidy and easy to grab.
items.buying_tips: Match the saddle width to your dumbbell heads; A-frame trees suit small home sets.

items.name: Fractional plates
items.description: Small plates (0.25–2.5 kg, or 0.25–1.25 lb microplates) for tiny jumps in weight. Keep progress going on presses and curls.
items.weight_options: Change plates 0.5–2.5 kg; microplates 0.25–1 kg (0.25–1.25 lb); magnetic versions for dumbbells
items.buying_tips: A 0.25–1 kg set is cheap and lets you progress 0.5 kg at a time; magnetic micro-weights also work on dumbbells.
items.keywords: fractional micro change plates small increments

items.name: Freestanding digital home gym
items.description: A floor-standing unit with two motorised cable arms, a screen and usually a folding bench and bar. Rolls away when not in use.
items.adjustability: Arms adjust height and angle; bench folds.
items.buying_tips: Compare peak load, cable length and noise; check the warranty on the motors.

items.name: Plate tree
items.description: A stand with pegs that holds weight plates, often with bar holders. Keeps plates off the floor and easy to reach.
items.buying_tips: Look for wheels and bar holders; rack-mounted plate horns save floor space.
items.safety: Load evenly to avoid tipping.

items.name: Plate-loaded cable tower
items.description: A freestanding cable tower or functional trainer with plate horns instead of a weight stack. Cheaper and lighter to ship than stack units.
items.adjustability: Adjustable pulley carriages; some have fixed high/low only.
items.buying_tips: Small plates (1.25–2.5 kg) matter more here because cable moves need small jumps.

items.name: Plate-loaded leverage gym
items.description: A multi-gym that loads plates on lever arms instead of a stack, with press, row, pulldown and leg stations. Feels more like commercial plate-loaded machines.
items.adjustability: Adjustable seat and arm start positions.
items.buying_tips: Check the plate horn size (50 mm Olympic) and that the lever arms move independently if you want unilateral work.

items.name: Power tower
items.description: A free-standing tower combining a pull-up bar, dip handles, a back-padded knee-raise station and often push-up handles.
items.buying_tips: Wider, heavier bases wobble less; check ceiling height for full pull-ups.
items.safety: Avoid kipping on free-standing towers, which can rock or tip.
items.keywords: power tower pull up dip station vkr

items.name: Rack-mounted cable arms
items.description: A pair of adjustable pulley carriages and stacks or plate horns that mount to the uprights of a power rack, turning it into a functional trainer.
items.weight_options: Plate horns or 70–90 kg stacks per side
items.adjustability: Pulleys slide on the rack uprights.
items.buying_tips: Plate-loaded kits are cheaper; check the cable ratio and that your rack is deep enough.

items.name: Single-stack cable tower
items.description: One weight stack with a single pulley that slides along a vertical column. Does nearly every cable exercise one side at a time.
items.adjustability: Pulley adjusts in height; some rotate.
items.buying_tips: A good space-saver if you do not need two-handle flys; check the top pulley clears your height for pulldowns.
items.safety: Bolt or weight the base if the manual says so.

items.name: Smith / functional trainer combo
items.description: A single frame combining a Smith machine, a power rack, dual adjustable cable pulleys, lat pulldown and low row, and a pull-up bar. Popular for complete home gyms.
items.weight_options: Two 70–100 kg stacks or plate horns; Smith bar 10–20 kg
items.adjustability: Adjustable pulleys, J-hooks, safeties and Smith hooks.
